newsitem.title: USA: GE boosts dividend, splits stock.
newsitem.headline: GE boosts dividend, splits stock.

text.p: In a widely expected move, General Electric Co. on Thursday increased its quarterly dividend and share repurchase programme and announced a 2-for-1 stock split.

Market analysts said the move suggests the huge, well-oiled conglomerate -- whose business range from the NBC television network to aircraft engines and financial services -- is set to cruise through 1997 with only minor potholes on the road ahead.
"There's not a lot on the horizon that could result in a negative surprise," said Bill Fiala, capital goods analyst at Edward D. Jones in St. Louis.

"The fact that they continue to repurchase shares and support internal growth and make a number of sizable acquisitions -- and increase their dividend -- just reinforces that GE has a very strong cash flow," he said.
Fiala said the Fairfield, Conn.-based diversified giant should see annual earnings growth of 12 percent over the next five years.
"We have not even begun to see the tip of the iceberg in terms of GE's potential growth," said Nicholas Heyman, vice president of research at NatWest Securities Corp.
Heyman expects GE's compounded earnings per share to swell 17.6 percent from 1996 to 2000, after growing 11.2 percent from 1991 to 1995.
"Those are heady numbers for a company this size," he said, adding that the phenomenal increase was driven by actual sales growth as opposed to operating margin improvement.

Working in GE's favour is its push to expand all its businesses overseas, its shift to sell more services to existing manufacturing and equipment customers, and its emphasis on improved production quality, said Heyman.

"The magic of this company is the diversification, and the market seems to be willing to pay for that," said a Wall Street analyst. GE has major businesses in power generators, appliances, lighting, plastics, medical systems, aircraft engines, financial services and broadcasting.

The Wall Street analyst said GE has a penchant for tight control, as reflected in the stock buyback and dividend increase. "People can get a little distressed at GE's control, but the bottom line is that only good companies are able to exercise control," she said.

"GE has good prospects in many global markets and a management philosophy that they are never satisfied with what they have, which is healthy," said Steve O'Neil, vice president at J.J.B. Hilliard-W.L. Lyons in Louisville, Ken.
"They are so diversified that it's hard to think of a single (negative) event that could affect all their businesses in a specific way," said O'Neil.

A GE spokesman said the company was on track to meet analysts' expectations of $7.2 billion to $7.3 billion in earnings this year, which could give GE the highest profits of any company in the United States for the first time.
"We obviously have good strong momentum," said GE spokesman Bruce Bunch. "I think we'll see continued good growth."
Bunch declined to give specific projections.

One Wall Street analyst said GE's main pitfalls ahead were in broadcasting and plastics. "The network business is cyclical, and GE can't rely on the fact that (NBC competitors) ABC and CBS will be asleep at the switch forever," she said.
Plastics is increasingly a commodity industry, with pricing beyond the control of manufacturers, she added.
